title: Medicaid 101: How America's Safety Net Works
subtitle: Eligibility, financing, managed care, waivers, and the future of the program
description: A comprehensive introduction to Medicaid — the largest source of health coverage in the United States. Covers program structure, eligibility rules, federal-state financing, managed care, waiver authority, quality oversight, and current policy debates. Essential for anyone working in health policy, state government, managed care, community health, or advocacy.
targetAudience: Anyone new to US health system financing

tracks.title: Medicaid Foundations
tracks.description: History, purpose, and scope of the Medicaid program — from its 1965 origins through the ACA expansion.

lessons.title: Medicaid's Origins: 1965 to Today
lessons.summary: How Medicaid was born alongside Medicare in 1965, its evolution through welfare reform, and the ACA's transformative expansion.

objectives.text: Explain why Medicaid was created as a separate program from Medicare
Describe the key legislative milestones from 1965 to the ACA
Explain what the ACA Medicaid expansion changed and why some states did not expand

contentBlocks.heading: Two programs, one moment
contentBlocks.body:
On July 30, 1965, President Lyndon Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments in Independence, Missouri — with Harry Truman seated beside him. The legislation created two programs at once: Medicare (Title XVIII), covering the elderly regardless of income, and Medicaid (Title XIX), covering certain low-income populations through a federal-state partnership.

The distinction mattered politically. Medicare was framed as earned insurance — workers paid in, workers got benefits. Medicaid was framed as welfare — means-tested assistance for the deserving poor. That framing has shaped every policy debate about the program since.

items.title: Title XIX enacted
items.body: Medicaid created as joint federal-state program. Initial enrollment: ~4 million people.

items.title: SSI integration
items.body: Supplemental Security Income created; Medicaid automatically linked to SSI recipients in most states.

items.title: Mandatory expansions
items.body: Congress mandates coverage for pregnant women and children up to 133% FPL, decoupling Medicaid from welfare cash assistance.

items.title: CHIP created
items.body: State Children's Health Insurance Program (Title XXI) created, covering children in families above Medicaid limits.

items.title: ACA enacted
items.body: ACA expands Medicaid to all adults under 138% FPL; federal government pays 100% of expansion costs through 2016, then 90% permanently.

items.title: NFIB v. Sebelius
items.body: Supreme Court rules ACA Medicaid expansion is effectively optional for states. 10 states still have not expanded as of 2025.

items.title: Unwinding begins
items.body: Post-COVID continuous enrollment protection ends; states begin redetermining eligibility for ~90 million enrollees.

contentBlocks.caption: Medicaid at a glance — Kaiser Family Foundation overview (~7 min)

contentBlocks.heading: Medicaid is not one program
contentBlocks.body: Each state runs its own Medicaid program within federal guidelines. Vermont's program (Green Mountain Care) looks very different from Texas's. Eligibility rules, covered services, payment rates, and delivery systems all vary. When someone says 'Medicaid,' they often mean something specific to their state.

questions.question: What did the Supreme Court's 2012 NFIB v. Sebelius ruling determine about the ACA Medicaid expansion?
questions.explanation: The Court ruled states could not be coerced into expanding Medicaid by threat of losing all existing federal Medicaid funding — making expansion effectively optional.

options.text: The ACA Medicaid expansion was unconstitutional and struck down entirely
States could not be forced to expand Medicaid — making expansion optional
All states were required to expand Medicaid by 2014
The federal match rate for expansion was reduced from 90% to 75%

questions.question: What share of US births does Medicaid cover?

options.text: About 20%
About 40%
About 60%
About 15%

lessons.title: Who Medicaid Covers: Populations & Benefits
lessons.summary: The mandatory and optional populations Medicaid must and may cover, and the mandatory vs. optional benefits framework.

objectives.text: Distinguish mandatory from optional Medicaid populations
List the mandatory Medicaid benefits all states must cover
Explain why benefits vary so much across states

contentBlocks.heading: Not everyone who is poor qualifies
contentBlocks.body:
A common misconception: Medicaid covers all low-income people. It does not. Medicaid covers specific *categories* of low-income people — and until the ACA, childless adults were largely excluded regardless of income.

The ACA changed this for expansion states by creating a new adult group (ages 19–64, income ≤138% FPL) with no categorical requirement. But even today, in non-expansion states, a working-age adult without children and without a disability may have no path to Medicaid regardless of how poor they are.

contentBlocks.heading: Mandatory Medicaid populations (all states must cover)

items.title: Children
items.body: Children in families up to 138% FPL. CHIP covers additional children up to state-set limits, often 200–300% FPL.

items.title: Pregnant women
items.body: Pregnant women up to 138% FPL for pregnancy-related services. Many states cover up to 200% FPL.

items.title: People with disabilities
items.body: SSI recipients are automatically enrolled in most states. Covers significant long-term services and supports.

items.title: Low-income seniors
items.body: "Dual eligibles" — people with both Medicare and Medicaid. Medicaid covers Medicare premiums, cost-sharing, and long-term care.

items.title: Foster care youth
items.body: Children in foster care and, under ACA, former foster youth up to age 26.

items.title: ACA adult group
items.body: In expansion states: non-pregnant adults 19–64 with income ≤138% FPL, no categorical requirement.

contentBlocks.heading: EPSDT is a powerful children's benefit
contentBlocks.body: Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) requires states to cover any medically necessary service for children under 21 — even if that service is optional for adults. This makes children's Medicaid benefits significantly broader than adult benefits in many states.

questions.question: Are prescription drugs a mandatory Medicaid benefit that all states must cover?
questions.explanation: Prescription drugs are technically an optional benefit — but all 50 states and DC cover them because formulary drug coverage is practically essential and federal law provides strong rebate incentives.

options.text: Yes, all states are required to cover prescription drugs
No, prescription drugs are optional — but all states cover them in practice
Only generic drugs are mandatory; brand-name drugs are optional
Prescription drugs are only covered for children under Medicaid

tracks.title: Eligibility & Enrollment
tracks.description: How income is calculated using MAGI, the redetermination process, the coverage gap in non-expansion states, and the post-COVID unwinding.

lessons.title: How Medicaid Eligibility Works: MAGI & Income Rules
lessons.summary: Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI), the 5% income disregard, household composition rules, and the difference between Medicaid and marketplace eligibility.

objectives.text: Explain what MAGI is and why the ACA standardized it for Medicaid
Calculate whether a hypothetical household is Medicaid-eligible
Describe the coverage gap and who it affects

contentBlocks.heading: Before the ACA: a patchwork of rules
contentBlocks.body: Before 2014, each state used its own income-counting methodology — some used gross income, others net income, others deducted specific expenses. A person could be eligible in Vermont but not New Hampshire even with identical income. The ACA standardized eligibility for most groups using Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) — the same concept used for federal tax purposes.

contentBlocks.heading: What MAGI includes (and excludes)
contentBlocks.body:
MAGI for Medicaid = Adjusted Gross Income (from federal tax return) + untaxed foreign income + tax-exempt interest + non-taxable Social Security benefits.

Notably excluded: assets. Unlike the old Medicaid rules, MAGI-based eligibility does not count savings accounts, home equity, or car values. A person with $50,000 in a savings account can qualify if their income is low enough. (This does not apply to long-term care Medicaid — asset tests still apply there.)

The ACA also added a standard 5% FPL income disregard — effectively raising the income limit by 5 percentage points. So a state with a 133% FPL limit actually covers people up to 138% FPL in practice.

stats.label: FPL — ACA adult expansion limit (with 5% disregard)
People in the coverage gap (non-expansion states, 2024)
States that have not expanded Medicaid as of 2025

contentBlocks.heading: The coverage gap: when you're too poor for help
contentBlocks.body: In non-expansion states, adults without children or disabilities often fall into a 'coverage gap': they earn too much for traditional Medicaid (which may have limits well below 100% FPL) but too little for ACA marketplace subsidies (which start at 100% FPL). An estimated 2.5 million people are trapped in this gap — poor enough that they can't afford coverage, but ineligible for either program.

contentBlocks.label: Eligibility worker perspective: common misconceptions
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a Medicaid eligibility worker or navigator about the top misconceptions applicants have about income rules, asset tests, and the application process. Recommended: 5–8 minutes.

questions.question: Under MAGI-based Medicaid eligibility, does a $40,000 savings account disqualify an otherwise eligible applicant?
questions.explanation: MAGI-based Medicaid does not count assets — only income. Asset tests were eliminated for most Medicaid groups under the ACA. (Exception: long-term care Medicaid still has asset rules.)

options.text: Yes, assets above $2,000 disqualify applicants
No, MAGI-based eligibility does not count assets
Only retirement accounts are excluded; regular savings count
Assets are counted but only above $10,000

questions.question: The 'coverage gap' in non-expansion states affects people who:

options.text: Earn too much for marketplace subsidies but too little for Medicaid
Earn too much for traditional Medicaid but too little for marketplace subsidies
Are eligible for both Medicaid and Medicare simultaneously
Have pre-existing conditions that disqualify them from marketplace plans

lessons.title: The Great Unwinding: Post-COVID Redeterminations
lessons.summary: How the COVID continuous enrollment protection worked, what the unwinding meant for states and enrollees, and lessons for eligibility modernization.

objectives.text: Explain what the continuous enrollment condition was and why it ended
Describe the scale of the unwinding and its equity implications
Identify policy lessons for reducing inappropriate disenrollment

contentBlocks.heading: The freeze and the thaw
contentBlocks.body:
In March 2020, the Families First Coronavirus Response Act included a provision: states could receive enhanced federal matching funds (a 6.2 percentage point FMAP increase) in exchange for maintaining continuous enrollment — they could not disenroll anyone from Medicaid during the public health emergency, even if their circumstances changed.

Enrollment surged from ~71 million to ~94 million. The continuous enrollment protection ended April 1, 2023. States had 12 months to complete redeterminations for everyone. The process — called the 'unwinding' — became one of the largest eligibility events in Medicaid history.

stats.label: Of disenrollments due to procedural reasons (not income)
Months states had to complete redeterminations

contentBlocks.heading: Most disenrollments were procedural
contentBlocks.body: The majority of people losing Medicaid coverage during the unwinding were disenrolled for procedural reasons — outdated addresses, returned mail, inability to reach enrollees — not because they were actually ineligible. Many were still poor enough to qualify but lost coverage anyway. This highlighted structural failures in state eligibility systems.

contentBlocks.caption: Medicaid unwinding — KFF explainer on the redetermination process (~6 min)

questions.question: What was the primary reason most people lost Medicaid coverage during the 2023–2024 unwinding?
questions.explanation: Studies found that roughly 70% of disenrollments were for procedural reasons — outdated contact information, returned mail, etc. — not because enrollees were actually ineligible.

options.text: They found jobs and their income rose above the eligibility limit
Procedural reasons: outdated addresses, returned mail, unreachable enrollees
They voluntarily switched to employer-sponsored insurance
Congress reduced the income eligibility threshold during the unwinding

tracks.title: Federal-State Financing
tracks.description: How Medicaid is funded: FMAP, the federal match, state budgets, and the politics of federal funding formulas.

lessons.title: The Federal Match: How FMAP Works
lessons.summary: The Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP), how it is calculated, why it varies by state, and what enhanced FMAPs mean for state budgets.

objectives.text: Define FMAP and explain how it is calculated
Explain why richer states have lower FMAPs
Describe the enhanced FMAP for ACA expansion and its fiscal significance

contentBlocks.heading: Every Medicaid dollar is matched
contentBlocks.body:
Medicaid is an entitlement program with open-ended federal funding. For every dollar a state spends on covered services for eligible beneficiaries, the federal government pays back a share — the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage (FMAP).

FMAP is calculated based on each state's per capita income relative to the national average. Poorer states get higher federal matches (up to 83%); wealthier states get lower matches (the statutory floor is 50%). Vermont's FMAP is approximately 56%; Mississippi's is approximately 77%.

This design is redistributive: federal dollars flow disproportionately to states with lower income — and lower tax capacity — giving them a stronger safety net than they could afford alone.

contentBlocks.heading: Enhanced FMAPs reward state action
contentBlocks.body: Congress has used enhanced FMAPs as policy levers: COVID-19 added 6.2 points, ACA expansion gets a permanent 90% match, and the American Rescue Plan offered states a 5-point increase if they expanded Medicaid. The fiscal incentive is powerful — a state covering one new expansion enrollee at 90% federal match only risks 10 cents of state money per dollar spent.

contentBlocks.heading: Block grants vs. the current structure
contentBlocks.body: Periodically, Congress debates converting Medicaid to a block grant — a fixed annual payment to states regardless of enrollment or spending. Proponents argue it gives states flexibility and controls federal spending. Opponents note that the current open-ended match is counter-cyclical: federal support automatically increases during recessions when enrollment grows and state revenues fall. A block grant would shift this recession risk entirely to states.

questions.question: Why do poorer states receive a higher FMAP than wealthier states?
questions.explanation: FMAP is inversely related to state per capita income — states with lower average incomes receive higher federal matches because they have less tax capacity to finance their share of Medicaid.

options.text: Poorer states have more Medicaid enrollees, so they need more federal help
FMAP is inversely related to per capita income — poorer states have less tax capacity
Federal law requires all states to receive the same FMAP
Poorer states negotiate higher FMAPs based on their Medicaid quality scores

tracks.title: Managed Care
tracks.description: How most states deliver Medicaid through managed care organizations, capitated payments, network adequacy, and quality requirements.

lessons.title: MCOs: Capitation, Networks & Accountability
lessons.summary: How Medicaid managed care organizations are paid, contracted, and held accountable — and why states moved from fee-for-service to managed care.

objectives.text: Explain how capitated managed care differs from fee-for-service
Describe how states set capitation rates and what actuarial soundness means
Identify the key accountability mechanisms for Medicaid MCOs

contentBlocks.heading: The shift to managed care
contentBlocks.body:
In 1980, nearly all Medicaid was delivered fee-for-service: states paid providers directly for each covered service. By 2023, approximately 72% of Medicaid beneficiaries — and 55% of Medicaid spending — flows through managed care organizations (MCOs).

The shift happened for several reasons: states wanted cost predictability, MCOs promised care coordination, and federal law in the 1990s made it easier for states to mandate managed care enrollment without federal waivers.

rows.label: Payment model
rows.right: State pays MCO fixed monthly amount per member (PMPM)

rows.label: Financial risk
rows.right: MCO bears utilization risk within contracted services

rows.label: Provider payment
rows.right: MCO sets rates within contract minimums

contentBlocks.heading: Actuarial soundness: the legal floor
contentBlocks.body: Federal law requires that Medicaid capitation rates be 'actuarially sound' — sufficient to pay for covered services for the enrolled population. States must document their actuarial basis. Rates that are too low create financial pressure on MCOs that can result in inadequate provider networks, prior authorization barriers, or insolvency.

items.title: Contracts
items.body: State-MCO contracts specify covered services, network requirements, quality measures, and financial penalties for non-compliance.

items.title: HEDIS measures
items.body: MCOs report standardized quality measures (HEDIS). States may tie a portion of capitation to performance on key measures.

items.title: Network adequacy
items.body: Federal rules require MCOs to maintain sufficient providers (time/distance standards) so enrollees can access covered services.

items.title: MLR requirements
items.body: MCOs must spend at least 85% of premium revenue on medical costs (medical loss ratio). Excess profit must be returned to the state.

contentBlocks.label: MCO perspective: managing Medicaid populations
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a Medicaid MCO medical director or care coordinator about the realities of managing complex populations, prior authorization challenges, and value-based contracting with providers. Recommended: 8–10 minutes.

questions.question: What does 'actuarially sound' mean for Medicaid capitation rates?
questions.explanation: Actuarial soundness means rates must be sufficient to pay for covered services for the enrolled population, based on documented actuarial analysis.

options.text: Rates must be lower than what Medicare pays for the same services
Rates must be sufficient to cover expected costs for the enrolled population
Rates must be approved by the state insurance commissioner
Rates must include a 15% profit margin for the MCO

tracks.title: Waivers & State Flexibility
tracks.description: Section 1115 waivers, HCBS waivers, and how states use federal waiver authority to test new approaches and cover populations beyond standard rules.

lessons.title: Section 1115 Waivers: Laboratories of Democracy
lessons.summary: How Section 1115 demonstration waivers allow states to test Medicaid expansions, restrictions, and innovations — and the political battles over work requirements.

objectives.text: Explain what a Section 1115 waiver is and what it allows states to do
Describe the 'budget neutrality' requirement for 1115 waivers
Analyze the work requirements debate and court rulings

contentBlocks.heading: Waiver authority: flexibility within a framework
contentBlocks.body:
Section 1115 of the Social Security Act gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to waive almost any Medicaid requirement for 'experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects' that promote the program's objectives.

States apply to CMS with a proposed innovation, CMS negotiates terms, and if approved, the state gets a five-year waiver (renewable). The waiver must be 'budget neutral' — the federal government should spend no more than it would have without the waiver.

This has been used for expansive purposes (covering childless adults before the ACA, adding dental benefits) and restrictive ones (imposing work requirements, charging premiums, limiting retroactive coverage).

contentBlocks.heading: Work requirements: blocked by the courts
contentBlocks.body: Several Republican administrations approved 1115 waivers requiring Medicaid enrollees to document work, volunteering, or job training to maintain coverage. Courts repeatedly struck these down, ruling that work requirements do not promote Medicaid's objective of providing health coverage — they undermine it by causing coverage loss. The legal and policy debate continues.

contentBlocks.heading: What states have used 1115 waivers to do

items.title: Cover new populations
items.body: Cover childless adults, undocumented immigrants for emergency care, or people above standard income limits.

items.title: Add benefits
items.body: Add dental, vision, or housing supports beyond standard Medicaid services.

items.title: Impose cost-sharing
items.body: Charge premiums or copays to groups that otherwise wouldn't pay them.

items.title: Work requirements
items.body: Require documentation of employment or community engagement — legally contested and often blocked.

items.title: Housing supports
items.body: Pay for transitional housing and housing navigation as health-related services.

items.title: Restructure delivery
items.body: Create integrated managed care systems, global budgets, or value-based payment models.

questions.question: What does 'budget neutrality' require for a Section 1115 waiver?
questions.explanation: Budget neutrality means the federal government cannot spend more under the waiver than it would have under standard Medicaid rules — any expansion in benefits or populations must be offset by savings elsewhere.

options.text: The state must balance its Medicaid budget before applying for the waiver
The federal government should spend no more with the waiver than without it
The state must match federal spending dollar-for-dollar
CMS must certify that the waiver will save money within five years

lessons.title: HCBS Waivers: Care at Home Instead of in Institutions
lessons.summary: How Home and Community-Based Services waivers let Medicaid pay for care in homes and communities rather than nursing facilities — and the long waitlists that result.

objectives.text: Explain what HCBS waivers are and why they were created
Describe the institutional bias in Medicaid and why it persists
Understand the HCBS waitlist problem and its equity implications

contentBlocks.heading: The institutional bias
contentBlocks.body:
Federal Medicaid law has historically required states to cover nursing facility care for eligible seniors and people with disabilities — but did not require states to cover equivalent care at home. This created an institutional bias: you could get a nursing home bed covered, but not the home aide that would let you stay in your own house.

Section 1915(c) HCBS waivers were created in 1981 to let states pay for home and community-based care as an alternative to institutionalization. States can cap enrollment (unlike nursing home coverage, which is an entitlement), which has created massive waitlists in many states.

stats.label: People on HCBS Medicaid waitlists nationally
Average daily cost of nursing facility care vs. ~$200 for home care
Of nursing home residents covered by Medicaid
American Rescue Plan investment in HCBS (2021)

contentBlocks.heading: Money follows the person
contentBlocks.body: 'Money Follows the Person' (MFP) is a CMS demonstration program that helps people transition from nursing facilities back to community settings. When someone leaves a nursing facility for home care, their Medicaid funding moves with them. Vermont has been a national leader in this model.

questions.question: Why can states cap HCBS waiver enrollment but cannot cap nursing facility coverage?
questions.explanation: Nursing facility coverage is a mandatory Medicaid benefit — an entitlement that eligible people have a legal right to. HCBS waivers are optional and capped, which is why waitlists exist.

options.text: HCBS is more expensive than nursing facility care
Nursing facility coverage is a mandatory entitlement; HCBS waivers are optional and capped
Federal law prohibits unlimited HCBS spending
HCBS providers have limited capacity and cannot accept unlimited referrals

tracks.title: Quality & Oversight
tracks.description: How CMS and states measure Medicaid quality, HEDIS measures, CHIP reauthorization quality initiatives, and the push for value-based payment in Medicaid.

lessons.title: Measuring Medicaid Quality: HEDIS, CAHPS & State Reporting
lessons.summary: How Medicaid quality is measured and reported, the role of HEDIS measures, member experience surveys, and CMS's push toward value-based payment.

objectives.text: Identify the key Medicaid quality measures and why they matter
Explain how value-based payment is being introduced into Medicaid managed care
Describe what CAHPS measures and how member experience data is used

contentBlocks.heading: The quality measurement challenge
contentBlocks.body:
Medicaid serves populations with significant health complexity — high rates of chronic conditions, behavioral health needs, social determinants challenges, and limited prior access to care. Measuring quality in this context requires measures that account for acuity and capture what matters to enrollees.

CMS requires states to collect and report standardized quality data through the Medicaid and CHIP Quality Improvement Program (Medicaid managed care rules) and state reporting to CMS's Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System (T-MSIS).

items.title: Child immunizations
items.body: Childhood Immunization Status (CIS) — one of the most watched pediatric quality measures in Medicaid.

items.title: Prenatal & postpartum care
items.body: Timely prenatal visits, postpartum follow-up at 7–84 days. Critical given Medicaid's role covering 40% of births.

items.title: Behavioral health follow-up
items.body: Follow-up after ED visit for mental illness, follow-up after hospitalization for mental illness (FUH/FUM).

items.title: Medication adherence
items.body: PDC measures for diabetes, hypertension, and cholesterol medications — linked to long-term outcomes.

items.title: CAHPS
items.body: Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems — member experience surveys covering access, communication, and care coordination.

items.title: Prevention
items.body: Cervical cancer screening, colorectal cancer screening, diabetes eye exams — preventive services often underprovided to Medicaid populations.

contentBlocks.heading: Value-based payment in Medicaid managed care
contentBlocks.body: CMS increasingly pushes states to include value-based payment (VBP) requirements in MCO contracts. Under VBP, MCOs pass some financial risk to providers — paying primary care practices based on quality and outcomes rather than pure volume. Vermont's OneCare model is a leading example of provider-level VBP within a Medicaid context.

contentBlocks.label: Quality director perspective: measuring what matters
contentBlocks.hint: Interview a Medicaid MCO or state quality director about the practical challenges of quality measurement — data gaps, attribution, adjusting for social determinants. Recommended: 6–8 minutes.

questions.question: What does CAHPS measure in the Medicaid context?
questions.explanation: CAHPS (Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems) measures member experience — how enrollees perceive access to care, communication with providers, and care coordination quality.

options.text: Clinical outcomes like hospital readmission rates and mortality
Member experience: access, communication, and care coordination as perceived by enrollees
Financial performance of Medicaid MCOs
Provider compliance with network adequacy standards
